name: Larry Ellison
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Ellison founded Software Development Laboratories (precursor to Oracle) in 1977 at age 33, and Oracle's first commercial database shipped in 1979.
early_history_summary: Ellison dropped out of the University of Illinois after his sophomore year and briefly attended the University of Chicago before moving to Berkeley, California in 1966 to work as a computer programmer at various companies including Wells Fargo, Amdahl, and Ampex. By age 26 (1970) he was a mid-career programmer with no founding or notable product achievement.
family_context_summary: Born to a single mother in the Bronx and adopted by her aunt and uncle; raised in a lower-middle-class Jewish family in Chicago's South Side with a difficult relationship with his adoptive father.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; adoptive father was not in a tech or business domain.
evidence_summary: Ellison's path to Oracle began at age 33 in 1977, well past the age-26 threshold. Before that, he worked as a programmer at Ampex and Amdahl, gaining database experience but without any founding, notable product, or commercial success milestone by age 26.

name: Robert Woodrow Wilson
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Wilson earned his PhD from Caltech in 1962 at age 26, but the cosmic microwave background discovery with Penzias came in 1964 at age 28. A PhD alone is not a material milestone.
early_history_summary: Wilson earned his BA from Rice University in 1957 and his PhD from Caltech in 1962, doing radio astronomy research at the Owens Valley Radio Observatory under John Bolton and Maarten Schmidt. He joined Bell Laboratories in 1963, where he later discovered the CMB.
evidence_summary: Wilson completed his PhD at age 26 in 1962, but his Nobel Prize-winning discovery of the cosmic microwave background radiation occurred in 1964 at age 28. No seminal publication, notable product, or significant discovery is documented by age 26.

name: Gerd Binnig
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Binnig earned his bachelor's degree in 1973 and his PhD in 1978 at age 31. The scanning tunneling microscope was developed in 1981 at age 34, and the Nobel Prize came in 1986.
early_history_summary: Binnig studied physics at Goethe University Frankfurt, earning a bachelor's in 1973 and a PhD in 1978 on superconductivity. He joined IBM Zurich Research Laboratory in 1978, where he met Heinrich Rohrer and began the work that led to the STM.
family_context_summary: Born in Frankfurt am Main; family lived partly in Frankfurt and partly in Offenbach. His mother introduced him to classical music early in life. He played in a beat-band during his student years.
evidence_summary: Binnig had only a bachelor's degree by age 26 (1973). His PhD came at 31, the STM at 34, and the Nobel Prize at 39. No material milestone is documented by age 26.

name: Tim Berners-Lee
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Berners-Lee wrote the 'Enquire' program at CERN in 1980 at age 25, but it was a private, unpublished tool. The World Wide Web proposal came in 1989 at age 33, and the first web browser/server in December 1990 at age 35.
early_history_summary: Berners-Lee studied physics at Oxford University, graduating in 1976. He worked as an engineer at various companies before a six-month consulting stint at CERN in 1980, where he wrote 'Enquire,' a private notebook program. His seminal WWW work began in 1989.
family_context_summary: Born in London, the son of mathematicians and computer scientists Mary Lee Berners-Lee and Conway Berners-Lee, who worked on early computers including the Ferranti Mark 1.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were mathematicians and computer scientists who worked on early computing, providing significant domain proximity and intellectual environment from childhood.
evidence_summary: Berners-Lee's 'Enquire' program at CERN in 1980 (age 25) was a private, unpublished tool that formed the conceptual basis for the WWW but was not itself a material, independently verifiable milestone. His actual breakthrough—the WWW proposal, browser, and server—came in 1989-1990 at ages 33-35.

name: Anton Zeilinger
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Zeilinger earned his PhD from the University of Vienna in 1971 at age 26 with a thesis on neutron depolarization. His major quantum entanglement discoveries (GHZ states, quantum teleportation) came in the late 1980s-1990s. A PhD alone is not a material milestone.
early_history_summary: Zeilinger studied physics and mathematics at the University of Vienna from 1963 to 1971, earning his PhD in 1971 under Helmut Rauch. He worked as a research assistant at the Atominstitut Vienna from 1972 to 1979 and was a Fulbright Fellow at MIT before his habilitation in 1979.
family_context_summary: Born in 1945 in Ried im Innkreis, Upper Austria, Austria. Not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Zeilinger completed his PhD at age 26 in 1971, but his groundbreaking quantum entanglement work (GHZ states, quantum teleportation) came decades later in the late 1980s and 1990s. No seminal publication or significant discovery is documented by age 26.

name: Jeff Bezos
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Bezos graduated from Princeton in 1986 at age 22 and worked at Fitel, Bankers Trust, and D.E. Shaw. He became D.E. Shaw's youngest senior VP at age 30 and founded Amazon in 1994 at age 30.
early_history_summary: Bezos graduated summa cum laude from Princeton in 1986 with a BSE in electrical engineering and computer science. He worked at Fitel (a fintech startup), then Bankers Trust as a product manager (1988-1990), then D.E. Shaw (1990-1994). By age 26 (1990), he was a rising finance professional but had no founding or notable product milestone.
family_context_summary: Born to a teenage mother, Jacklyn, and father Ted Jorgensen; adopted by stepfather Miguel Bezos, an engineer at Exxon. Family moved to Houston and then Miami. Middle-class upbringing with stepfather's engineering career providing stability.
parent_family_domain_summary: Stepfather Miguel Bezos was an engineer at Exxon, providing some technical domain proximity, though not directly in software or entrepreneurship.
evidence_summary: Bezos was a successful corporate employee by age 26 (1990), working as a product manager at Bankers Trust, but had not founded a company, shipped a notable product, or achieved commercial success independently. Amazon was founded in 1994 at age 30.

name: Jerome Isaac Friedman
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Friedman earned his PhD from the University of Chicago in 1956 at age 26, studying under Enrico Fermi. His Nobel Prize-winning quark experiments at SLAC ran from 1967 to 1973. A PhD alone is not a material milestone.
early_history_summary: Friedman studied at the University of Chicago on a full scholarship, earning his PhD in 1956 under Enrico Fermi (who died in 1954) and then John Marshall. His thesis involved proton polarization experiments using nuclear emulsion plates. He then worked at Stanford with Hofstadter before joining MIT in 1960.
family_context_summary: Born in Chicago to Russian immigrant parents; father repaired and sold sewing machines, mother worked in a garment factory. Parents had little formal education but valued scholarship and made sacrifices for their children's intellectual development, providing music and art lessons despite financial difficulties.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were immigrants with no scientific background but strongly valued education and intellectual development.
evidence_summary: Friedman completed his PhD at age 26 in 1956, but his Nobel Prize-winning deep inelastic scattering experiments that confirmed quarks ran from 1967 to 1973, when he was 37-43. No seminal publication or significant discovery is documented by age 26.

name: Michael Houghton
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Houghton entered PhD studies at King's College London in 1973 and graduated in 1977 at age 28. The hepatitis C discovery came in 1989 at age 40. By age 26 (1975), he was a PhD student with no notable publication or discovery.
early_history_summary: Houghton won a scholarship to Alleyn's School and studied biological sciences at the University of East Anglia (1969-1972). He then joined GD Searle & Co.'s research labs, registering for a PhD at King's College London in 1973 and graduating in 1977. His work on the human fibroblast interferon gene came after his PhD.
family_context_summary: Born in London in 1949 to a working-class family; his father was a truck driver and union official. He won a scholarship to a private high school (Alleyn's School).
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; father was a truck driver, no scientific domain background.
evidence_summary: Houghton was a PhD student at age 26 (1975), with his doctorate completed in 1977 at age 28. The hepatitis C virus discovery came in 1989 at age 40. No material milestone is documented by age 26.

name: Riccardo Giacconi
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Giacconi earned his PhD from the University of Milan in 1954 at age 23, then was a Fulbright fellow at Indiana University (1956-1958) and Princeton (1958-1959). He joined AS&E in 1959 and began X-ray astronomy work. The first detection of a stellar X-ray source (Sco X-1) came in June 1962 at age 31.
early_history_summary: Giacconi earned his doctorate in physics from the University of Milan in 1954, doing cosmic ray research at the Testa Grigia Observatory. He came to the US on a Fulbright fellowship, working at Indiana University and Princeton before joining American Science and Engineering (AS&E) in Cambridge, Massachusetts in 1959, where Bruno Rossi suggested he pursue X-ray astronomy.
family_context_summary: Born in Genoa, Italy, on October 6, 1931. Not documented in reviewed sources beyond birthplace.
evidence_summary: Giacconi had his PhD by age 23 (1954) but was still a postdoctoral fellow at age 26 (1957), working at Indiana University. His pioneering X-ray astronomy work began at AS&E in 1959 at age 28, and the first stellar X-ray source detection came in 1962 at age 31. No material milestone by age 26.

name: Avram Hershko
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Hershko started medical school in 1956, earned his MD in 1965 at age 28, and his PhD in 1969 at age 32. His Nobel Prize-winning ubiquitin work began in the late 1970s. By age 26 (1963), he was still a medical student.
early_history_summary: Hershko emigrated from Hungary to Israel in 1950 and settled in Jerusalem. He began studying at the Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School in 1956, falling in love with biochemistry during his basic science courses. He took a year off during medical studies to do research in Jacob Mager's lab, then completed his MD in 1965 and PhD in 1969.
family_context_summary: Born in Karcag, Hungary in 1937; family emigrated to Israel in 1950 and settled in Jerusalem. His wartime experiences as a child in Hungary shaped his personality and worldview.
evidence_summary: Hershko was still a medical student at age 26 (1963), seven years into his studies at Hebrew University. His MD came at 28, PhD at 32, and Nobel Prize-winning ubiquitin research in the late 1970s. No material milestone by age 26.

name: Albert Fert
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Fert earned his Master's from Ecole Normale Superieure in Paris in 1962 and was a teaching assistant at Universite de Grenoble (1962-1964). His first notable paper ('Two-Current Conduction in Nickel') was published in 1968 at age 30, and the GMR discovery came in 1988 at age 50.
early_history_summary: Fert studied at the Ecole Normale Superieure in Paris (1957-1962), earning Master's degrees in mathematics and physics. He was a teaching assistant at Universite de Grenoble from 1962 to 1964, did military service in 1964-1965, then began his doctoral thesis at Universite Paris-Sud under Ian Campbell in 1965, completing his Doctor of Physical Science in 1970.
evidence_summary: Fert was a teaching assistant at age 26 (1964), having just completed his Master's at ENS Paris. His doctoral thesis began in 1965, his first notable publication came in 1968 at age 30, and the GMR discovery in 1988 at age 50. No material milestone by age 26.

name: Carl Sagan
milestone_by_age_26: Completed PhD thesis at University of Chicago in 1960 at age 25, demonstrating that the greenhouse effect of a thick CO2 and water vapor atmosphere explains Venus's high surface temperature; published multiple papers in PNAS and the Astronomical Journal by age 25-26.
early_history_summary: Sagan entered the University of Chicago at age 16 on a full scholarship in 1951, earning his AB (1954), SB (1955), SM (1956), and PhD (1960) in astronomy and astrophysics under Gerard Kuiper. He was mentored by Enrico Fermi, Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, Harold Urey, and H.J. Muller, and published his first paper ('Radiation and the Origin of the Gene') in Evolution at age 22 in 1957. His thesis included the Venus greenhouse model and papers on organic matter on the Moon published in PNAS in 1960.
family_context_summary: Born in 1934 in a working-class Jewish neighborhood of Brooklyn, New York. His father Samuel Sagan immigrated from Ukraine and worked as a garment worker; his mother Rachel was described as a major influence. Parents encouraged his scientific curiosity despite modest means.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; parents were not scientists but encouraged intellectual curiosity.
primary_early_advantage_tags: elite university, multiple Nobel-caliber mentors, Fermi, Urey, Kuiper, Muller, early university entry at 16, space race, planetary science pioneer
evidence_summary: Sagan entered the University of Chicago at 16 on a full scholarship and was immersed in an extraordinary intellectual environment with mentors including Enrico Fermi, Harold Urey, H.J. Muller, and Gerard Kuiper. By age 25, he had completed his PhD with a significant theoretical model explaining Venus's high surface temperature via the greenhouse effect, and published papers in PNAS and the Astronomical Journal. His working-class background and early university entry at 16 suggest both adversity-driven urgency and exceptional early cognitive ability. The emerging space race provided a structural wave that amplified the significance of his planetary science work.
